claims.text: Layered oxide perovskite materials can transition from a non-superconducting state into a superconducting state under appropriate synthesis and thermal-treatment conditions.
Superconductivity in these materials results from enhanced electron-phonon coupling mediated by their layered crystal structures.
The initial layered oxide perovskite compounds are non-superconducting.
Controlled cooling in a specific oxygen environment induces phase ordering.
Controlling oxygen partial pressure during low-temperature treatment ensures proper stoichiometry and crystal ordering.
A layered crystal structure supports enhanced electron-phonon interactions.
Upon cooling, lattice vibrational modes facilitate electron pairing into Cooper pairs.
Formation of Cooper pairs leads to superconductivity when the critical temperature is reached.
The treated material will exhibit zero electrical resistance below its critical temperature.
The same oxide perovskite maintained at room temperature without specialized thermal treatment exhibits normal resistivity.
The proposed mechanism may not extend to non-layered superconductors or systems dominated by magnetic effects.
Failure of treated samples to show a sharp transition to zero resistance would refute the hypothesis.
